name: Hot Metal, Cold Print: Newspapers and Magazines
description: How type, telegraph wires and rotary presses made the daily paper, and how screens and feeds are now emptying the newsroom of its old power.

checkpoints.name: Type and ink
checkpoints.note: Gutenberg's press makes cheap print possible, and in time The Times in London, The Guardian in Manchester and The Times of India in Bombay turn news into a daily habit. The electric telegraph then lets reports travel faster than any messenger.

checkpoints.name: The mass press
checkpoints.note: Punch, The Illustrated London News, News of the World and The Economist join a market of readers, while Reuters sells telegraph news and The New York Times rises. Pulitzer and Hearst fight for readers, and the Linotype machine speeds up typesetting.

checkpoints.name: The magazine age
checkpoints.note: The Daily Mail and Pravda reach millions, and glossy titles such as Vogue, Time, Reader's Digest, The New Yorker and Life reshape what people read. Radio and the Pulitzer Prize arrive, and Le Monde is born from the war.

checkpoints.name: Print at its height
checkpoints.note: Newspapers uncover scandals, and the Watergate story shows their power. Weekly Shonen Jump sells in huge numbers in Japan and Charlie Hebdo keeps up satire in France, while television pulls away readers and advertising.

checkpoints.name: The feed
checkpoints.note: Punch closes in 2002 and The Illustrated London News in 2003. Life, a weekly only until 1972, ends its last run in 2007, and News of the World shuts in 2011, while Google Reader and Twitter move reading to screens and feeds.
